stem: The chapter compares the development experiences of India with two of its neighbours, namely:
solution: The chapter compares the development experiences of India with two of its major neighbours — China and Pakistan. All three countries (India, China, and Pakistan) started their development journeys around the same time (the late 1940s), and comparing them helps us understand different development strategies and outcomes. (China became a communist/socialist state in 1949; India and Pakistan became independent in 1947.) Understanding that the comparison is India vs China vs Pakistan is a prelims point. The chapter compares the development experiences of India with its neighbours China and Pakistan.

stem: India, China, and Pakistan all started their development paths at around the same time — the:
solution: India, China, and Pakistan all started their modern development paths (as nations pursuing planned development) at around the same time — the late 1940s: India and Pakistan became independent in 1947, and the People's Republic of China was established in 1949. Because all three began at roughly the same time (and faced somewhat similar initial conditions of poverty and backwardness), comparing how they developed over the following decades — with their different strategies — is instructive. Understanding that all three started around the late 1940s is a prelims point. India, China, and Pakistan all began their development paths around the same time — the late 1940s.

stem: China introduced major economic reforms (opening up its economy) in __________, well before India's 1991 reforms.
solution: China introduced its major economic reforms (opening up and liberalising its economy, moving toward a market-oriented system while remaining politically communist) in 1978 (under Deng Xiaoping) — well before India's reforms of 1991 (and Pakistan's reforms of 1988). China's earlier start on reforms (in 1978) gave it a head start, and its reforms (combined with its earlier build-up of infrastructure and human capital) helped it achieve very rapid economic growth in the following decades, faster than India. Understanding that China reformed in 1978 (before India) is a prelims point. China introduced its major economic reforms in 1978, well before India's 1991 reforms.

stem: In terms of economic growth over the past few decades, __________ has grown the fastest among the three countries.
solution: Among the three countries, China has grown the fastest — it has achieved spectacularly high and sustained economic growth over the past few decades (often around 8–10% a year), transforming itself into one of the world's largest and most powerful economies. India has also grown quite fast (especially after its 1991 reforms), though not as fast as China; and Pakistan has grown more slowly and less steadily. So the ranking of growth performance has generally been China (fastest), then India, then Pakistan. Understanding that China grew the fastest is a prelims point. China has grown the fastest among the three countries over the past few decades.

stem: One reason for China's rapid growth was that it built up strong __________ and human capital (through education and health) BEFORE its 1978 reforms.
solution: One important reason for China's rapid growth after 1978 was that, in the decades before its reforms, China had already built up a strong foundation of infrastructure (roads, power, etc.) and, crucially, human capital — through massive investments in education and health, which greatly improved the literacy, skills, and health of its people. So, when China opened up and reformed its economy in 1978, it already had a healthy, educated workforce and good infrastructure in place, which enabled it to make the most of the reforms and grow very rapidly. (This is often contrasted with India, which had not built up its human capital and infrastructure to the same extent.) Understanding that China's pre-reform investment in infrastructure and human capital aided its growth is a prelims point. China built up strong infrastructure and human capital (education, health) before its 1978 reforms, aiding its rapid growth.

stem: China's 'one-child policy' (a strict population-control measure) had the effect of:
options: drastically slowing the growth of China's population
solution: China's 'one-child policy' — a strict population-control measure (introduced in 1979) that generally limited most urban couples to having only one child — had the effect of drastically slowing the growth of China's population (sharply reducing the birth rate). This helped China control its population growth (so that the fruits of its economic growth were shared among a more slowly-growing population, raising per-capita income). However, the policy also had negative side-effects — such as a skewed sex ratio (a shortage of females, due to a preference for sons) and an ageing population (a growing proportion of old people). (China has since relaxed the policy.) India, by contrast, has followed a non-coercive family-planning approach, and its population has grown faster. Understanding the effect of China's one-child policy is a prelims-relevant point. China's 'one-child policy' drastically slowed the growth of China's population.

stem: In China, before the 1978 reforms, agriculture and industry were largely organised through __________ (collective/state ownership).
options: communes and state-owned enterprises (a command economy)
solution: In China, before the 1978 reforms, the economy was a communist command economy, and agriculture and industry were largely organised through collective and state ownership: farming was organised into large collective farms called 'communes' (where land was collectively owned and worked, not privately owned by individual farmers), and industry was run through state-owned enterprises (owned and controlled by the government). The state planned and controlled the economy centrally. The 1978 reforms began to change this — allowing more private incentive and market forces (e.g., breaking up the communes and letting farmers/enterprises produce and sell more freely) — which spurred China's growth. Understanding China's pre-reform command structure (communes, state enterprises) is a prelims-relevant point. Before 1978, China organised agriculture and industry through communes and state-owned enterprises (a command economy).

stem: In terms of the composition of GDP, in India the __________ sector contributes the largest share, whereas in China manufacturing/industry has a very large share.
solution: In terms of the composition/structure of GDP (the shares of the different sectors in national output): in India, the service (tertiary) sector contributes the largest share of GDP (India's growth has been led by services, like IT); whereas in China, the manufacturing/industry (secondary) sector has a very large share (China grew as a manufacturing powerhouse — 'the factory of the world'). So the two countries have followed somewhat different structural paths: India moving strongly into services, and China into manufacturing. (China's strong manufacturing base created a lot of employment and export strength; India's service-led growth created fewer jobs — a point of concern.) Understanding this difference (India service-led, China manufacturing-led) is a prelims point. In India, the service sector has the largest share of GDP, whereas in China manufacturing/industry has a very large share.

stem: In terms of human development indicators (like life expectancy, literacy), China generally performs __________ India.
solution: In terms of the human development indicators — such as life expectancy, literacy rate, infant mortality, and access to health and education — China generally performs better than India (China has, for example, higher life expectancy and literacy and lower infant mortality than India). This reflects China's greater and earlier investment in the education, health, and welfare of its people. (India lags behind China on many of these human-development measures, though it is ahead of, or comparable to, Pakistan on some.) So, on human development, the ranking is often China ahead, then India, then Pakistan (roughly). Understanding that China does better than India on human development indicators is a prelims point. China generally performs better than India on human development indicators (life expectancy, literacy, etc.).

stem: Pakistan's economic development has been hampered by factors such as political instability, over-dependence on __________, and remittances/foreign aid.
options: agriculture and a narrow range of exports/foreign loans
solution: Pakistan's economic development has been hampered/held back by several factors, including: political instability (frequent changes of government, including military rule, and a lack of consistent policies); an over-dependence on agriculture and on a narrow range of exports (and volatile agricultural performance); a heavy reliance on foreign loans/aid and on remittances (money sent home by Pakistanis working abroad, especially in the Gulf) — which are unstable sources; low investment in human development; and various internal conflicts and security problems. These factors have made Pakistan's growth slower and more erratic than India's or China's. Understanding the factors hampering Pakistan's development is a prelims-relevant point. Pakistan's development has been hampered by political instability, over-dependence on agriculture and a narrow export base, and reliance on remittances/foreign aid.

stem: One lesson from China's success (for India) is the importance of investing heavily in __________ (education, health, infrastructure) to support growth.
solution: One key lesson from China's success (for India, and other countries) is the importance of investing heavily in human capital (the education, health, and skills of the people) and infrastructure (roads, power, ports, etc.) — as China did, especially before its reforms — to build a strong foundation for rapid and sustained economic growth. China's healthy, educated workforce and good infrastructure enabled it to grow much faster than India after opening up. This suggests that India needs to do more to develop its human capital (improve education and health) and infrastructure, in order to accelerate its own growth and development. Understanding this lesson (invest in human capital and infrastructure) is a prelims-relevant point. A lesson from China's success is the importance of investing heavily in human capital (education, health) and infrastructure to support growth.

stem: Development should be judged not only by economic growth (GDP) but also by improvements in __________.
options: human welfare and human development (health, education, poverty reduction, equity, quality of life)
solution: A key insight from comparing development experiences is that development should be judged not only by economic growth (the rise in GDP/output) but also — and more importantly — by improvements in human welfare and human development: the health, education, and living standards of the people; the reduction of poverty and inequality; and the overall quality of life and well-being. High GDP growth is not enough if it does not translate into better lives for the people (especially the poor); conversely, genuine development means people living longer, healthier, better-educated, and more secure and dignified lives. So the comparison of India, China, and Pakistan is made not just on growth, but on human-development indicators too. Understanding that development is about human welfare (not just GDP) is a key prelims point. Development should be judged not only by economic growth (GDP) but also by improvements in human welfare and human development (health, education, poverty reduction, quality of life).

stem: Both China and India, despite their impressive growth, still face challenges such as:
options: poverty, inequality, and environmental problems (and, for China, some political/social issues; for India, human-development gaps)
solution: Both China and India, despite their impressive economic growth, still face significant challenges/problems, such as: poverty (large numbers of poor people still remain, especially in India, and in China's rural/interior areas); inequality (the gap between the rich and the poor, and between the developed and backward regions, has widened with growth); and serious environmental problems (pollution, resource depletion, and — especially for China as a huge industrial economy — severe environmental degradation). In addition, India faces gaps in human development (health, education) and job creation, and China faces issues like an ageing population and (a non-economic point) restrictions on political freedom. So growth alone has not solved all their problems — showing that development is an ongoing challenge. Understanding these continuing challenges is a prelims-relevant point. Despite their growth, both China and India still face challenges like poverty, inequality, and environmental problems.

stem: China's development strategy is often described as achieving rapid growth under a __________ political system (combining a market economy with one-party communist rule).
solution: China's development strategy is often described as achieving rapid economic growth under a one-party (authoritarian) communist political system — that is, China combined a shift toward a market-oriented economy (allowing private enterprise, foreign investment, and market forces, especially after 1978) with the retention of one-party (Communist Party) political control (an authoritarian, non-democratic political system). This is a distinctive combination (a market economy without political democracy). India, by contrast, has pursued development as a democracy (with political freedoms, multiple parties, and elections). This difference in political systems is one point of comparison (China's authoritarian system allowed it to push through decisions and reforms quickly, but at the cost of political and personal freedoms). Understanding China's model (market economy + one-party rule) is a prelims-relevant point. China achieved rapid growth under a one-party (authoritarian/communist) political system, combining a market economy with communist political rule.

stem: Assertion (A): China's early investment in health and education helped it grow rapidly after its 1978 reforms. Reason (R): A healthy, educated, and skilled workforce could take fuller advantage of the opportunities opened up by the reforms. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that China's early (pre-reform) investment in health and education (building up its human capital) helped it grow rapidly after its 1978 reforms. And the reason is (R) that, because it had built up a healthy, educated, and skilled workforce, China's people could take fuller advantage of the new opportunities opened up by the reforms — they could work productively in the new industries, adopt new technologies, and respond to the market opportunities, so the economy grew fast. In short, the human capital built earlier was what enabled the reforms to translate into rapid growth. So R correctly explains why the early investment in human capital helped China grow (A). Understanding this reasoning (human capital → ability to use reforms → fast growth) is a prelims point. China's early investment in health and education helped it grow fast after 1978 because a healthy, educated, skilled workforce could take fuller advantage of the reforms.

stem: The regional organisation of South Asian countries (including India, Pakistan, and others) for economic and regional cooperation is:
options: SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation)
solution: SAARC — the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation — is the regional organisation of the South Asian countries, established in 1985, for promoting economic, social, and regional cooperation among its members. Its members are India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, the Maldives, and Afghanistan. SAARC aims to accelerate the economic and social development of the region and foster cooperation among the neighbouring countries. (China is not a SAARC member, though it is an observer.) Understanding SAARC (South Asian regional cooperation) is a prelims-relevant point. SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation) is the regional organisation of South Asian countries including India and Pakistan.

stem: Pakistan introduced its economic reforms (liberalisation) in about __________, a few years before India.
solution: Pakistan introduced its economic reforms (its move toward liberalisation) in about 1988 — a few years before India's reforms of 1991 (and ten years after China's 1978 reforms). So among the three countries, China reformed first (1978), then Pakistan (1988), then India (1991). Understanding the timing of Pakistan's reforms (1988) is a prelims-relevant point. Pakistan introduced its economic reforms around 1988, a few years before India's 1991 reforms.

stem: China's disastrous campaign of 1958 (aimed at rapid industrialisation, which instead caused a great famine) was the:
solution: The 'Great Leap Forward' (launched in 1958 by Mao Zedong) was China's campaign aimed at rapidly industrialising the country and collectivising agriculture (through the communes). It was a disastrous failure: the forced collectivisation and the diversion of labour (e.g., to backyard steel furnaces) disrupted agriculture, and, combined with poor planning and bad weather, it led to a catastrophic famine (the Great Chinese Famine) in which millions of people died. It is an example of a development strategy that went badly wrong. (China later, after 1978, changed course to its successful market reforms.) Understanding the Great Leap Forward (1958, and its failure/famine) is a prelims-relevant point. The 'Great Leap Forward' (1958) was China's campaign for rapid industrialisation that instead caused a great famine.

stem: China's move (from 1978) that allowed individual farm households to keep and sell their surplus produce (replacing the collective communes) was the __________ system.
solution: The 'household responsibility system' was a key reform introduced in China's agriculture from 1978 (after the reforms began). Under it, the large collective communes were broken up, and individual farm households were given responsibility for plots of land — they had to meet certain quotas for the state, but they could keep and sell their surplus produce (beyond the quota) for themselves. This gave farmers a strong incentive to produce more (since they benefited directly from producing more), and it led to a big increase in agricultural production. It marked the shift from collective to more individual/market-based farming, and it was an important part of China's successful reforms. Understanding the household responsibility system is a prelims-relevant point. China's 'household responsibility system' (from 1978) let individual farm households keep and sell their surplus produce, replacing the collective communes.

stem: The rural industries that grew rapidly in China (owned by local communities/townships, absorbing rural labour) after the reforms were called:
solution: Township and Village Enterprises (TVEs) were the rural, community-owned enterprises (owned and run by the local townships and villages) that grew very rapidly in China after the reforms (in the 1980s). They set up small-scale industries and businesses in the rural areas, which: absorbed a huge amount of rural surplus labour (creating employment for people leaving agriculture, without them having to migrate to the big cities); boosted rural incomes and industrial production; and contributed greatly to China's growth. The success of the TVEs was an important feature of China's development (spreading industry and jobs to the rural areas). Understanding the TVEs is a prelims-relevant point. Township and Village Enterprises (TVEs) were China's rapidly-growing rural community-owned industries that absorbed rural labour after the reforms.

stem: China set up Special Economic Zones (SEZs) to attract foreign investment and boost exports; the FIRST and most famous of these was:
solution: China set up Special Economic Zones (SEZs) — special areas with liberal economic rules, tax incentives, and good infrastructure — to attract foreign investment and boost exports, as a key part of its reform strategy (its 'open-door policy'). The first and most famous of these SEZs was Shenzhen (near Hong Kong), which was transformed from a small fishing village into a booming industrial and export metropolis. The SEZs (Shenzhen and others) were hugely successful in bringing in foreign capital, technology, and export-oriented industry, powering China's growth. (India later also adopted the SEZ idea.) Understanding that Shenzhen was China's first/most famous SEZ is a prelims-relevant point. Shenzhen was China's first and most famous Special Economic Zone (SEZ), set up to attract foreign investment and boost exports.

stem: China's strategy of opening up to foreign trade and investment (a major part of its reforms) is often called its __________ policy.
solution: China's strategy of opening up its economy to foreign trade and foreign investment — reversing its earlier isolation and integrating with the world economy — is often called its 'open-door policy' (or 'opening up'). Introduced as part of the 1978 reforms (under Deng Xiaoping), it involved welcoming foreign investment (especially into the Special Economic Zones), promoting exports, and engaging in world trade. This open-door policy brought in foreign capital, technology, and markets, and it was central to China's transformation into a global manufacturing and export powerhouse. Understanding China's 'open-door policy' is a prelims-relevant point. China's strategy of opening up to foreign trade and investment is called its 'open-door policy'.

stem: China became known as the '__________ of the world' because of its huge manufacturing and export of goods.
solution: China became known as the 'factory of the world' because of its enormous manufacturing base and its massive production and export of manufactured goods to the whole world. By developing huge, competitive, export-oriented manufacturing industries (aided by cheap labour, good infrastructure, foreign investment, and the SEZs), China came to produce a vast share of the world's manufactured goods (from toys and clothes to electronics and machinery), which it exported globally — running large trade surpluses and building up huge foreign-exchange reserves. This manufacturing/export strength was central to China's rapid growth (and contrasts with India's more service-led growth). Understanding that China is the 'factory of the world' (manufacturing/export powerhouse) is a prelims-relevant point. China became known as the 'factory of the world' because of its huge manufacturing and export of goods.

stem: China has built up very large __________, reflecting its huge trade surpluses (exporting far more than it imports).
solution: China has built up very large foreign-exchange reserves — among the largest in the world — reflecting its huge trade surpluses (it exports far more than it imports, so foreign currency flows into the country). These massive reserves (and its export earnings) give China great economic strength and stability (and international influence). This is a result of China's export-led, manufacturing-based growth strategy. (India, by contrast, has often run trade deficits, though it too has built up sizeable reserves since the 1991 reforms.) Understanding China's large foreign-exchange reserves (from trade surpluses) is a prelims-relevant point. China has built up very large foreign-exchange reserves, reflecting its huge trade surpluses.

stem: China is the world's __________ largest economy (by GDP), after the United States.
solution: China is the world's second largest economy (by GDP/total output), after the United States (and, by some measures — purchasing power parity — even the largest). Its decades of rapid growth transformed it from a poor country into an economic superpower with the second-biggest economy in the world. (India, too, has risen to become one of the world's largest economies — around the fifth or sixth largest by total GDP — though still much smaller than China's, and with a much lower per-capita income.) Understanding China's position as the world's second-largest economy is a prelims-relevant point. China is the world's second-largest economy (by GDP), after the United States.

stem: In terms of POPULATION, China and India are the two __________ countries in the world.
solution: China and India are the two most populous countries in the world (the two largest by population) — together they account for a very large share (over a third) of the world's people. For a long time, China was the most populous and India the second; India has now overtaken China to become the most populous country (as China's population growth slowed sharply due to its one-child policy, while India's continued to grow). Their huge populations are a central feature of both countries' development challenges (and, potentially, their strength — as large workforces and markets). Understanding that China and India are the two most populous countries is a prelims point. China and India are the two most populous countries (largest by population) in the world.

stem: A negative side-effect of China's one-child policy has been a skewed (unbalanced) __________ and an ageing population.
solution: A negative side-effect of China's one-child policy (its strict population control) has been a skewed (unbalanced) sex ratio — a shortage of females relative to males. Because of a traditional preference for sons (and the limit of one child), many couples used sex-selective abortion or other means to ensure their one child was a boy, leading to far more males than females being born (a low ratio of females to males). Another negative consequence is an ageing population — with fewer children being born, the proportion of old people in the population has grown (and the working-age population is now shrinking), creating problems for the economy and for supporting the elderly. (These problems led China to relax the one-child policy.) Understanding these side-effects of the one-child policy (skewed sex ratio, ageing) is a prelims-relevant point. China's one-child policy caused a skewed sex ratio (shortage of females) and an ageing population.

stem: In India, a strength/advantage in its development has been its status as a functioning __________ (unlike China's one-party system).
solution: A strength/advantage of India (in its development experience) has been its status as a functioning democracy — with regular free elections, multiple political parties, freedom of speech and the press, an independent judiciary, and political and personal freedoms — unlike China's one-party (authoritarian) communist system. While an authoritarian system (like China's) can push through decisions and reforms quickly (which helped China's rapid growth), a democracy (like India's) provides freedom, accountability, participation, and the protection of rights — values important in themselves and for genuine, people-centred development. So India has pursued development within a democratic framework, which is a distinctive feature (and, many argue, a strength) of its experience. Understanding that India's democracy is a distinctive feature/strength is a prelims-relevant point. A strength of India is its status as a functioning democracy, unlike China's one-party authoritarian system.

stem: China's remarkable growth has lifted a very large number of its people out of __________.
solution: China's remarkable, sustained economic growth over the past few decades has lifted a very large number of its people out of poverty — hundreds of millions of Chinese have been raised out of extreme poverty, one of the most dramatic reductions in poverty in human history. This massive poverty reduction is one of the great achievements of China's development (made possible by its rapid, employment-generating, manufacturing-led growth). It illustrates how sustained high growth (if it creates jobs and reaches the people) can dramatically reduce poverty. (India too has reduced poverty, but less dramatically than China.) Understanding that China's growth greatly reduced poverty is a prelims-relevant point. China's remarkable growth has lifted a very large number (hundreds of millions) of its people out of poverty.

stem: A serious negative consequence of China's rapid industrial growth has been severe __________.
solution: A serious negative consequence of China's rapid, industry-heavy growth has been severe environmental degradation and pollution — China's cities and industrial regions suffer from some of the worst air pollution in the world (thick smog), along with widespread water pollution and land/soil degradation, resulting from its huge, energy- and coal-intensive manufacturing and construction. This heavy environmental cost is a downside of China's growth model (rapid growth pursued with less regard for the environment), and it poses serious health and sustainability problems (which China is now trying to address). It illustrates that growth achieved at the expense of the environment carries heavy hidden costs. Understanding China's severe pollution (a cost of its growth) is a prelims-relevant point. A serious negative consequence of China's rapid industrial growth has been severe environmental degradation and pollution.

stem: In the comparison, India's particular areas of strength include its __________ (a globally competitive sector).
solution: In the comparison, India's particular areas of strength include its information technology (IT) and software services sector — a globally competitive, world-class industry in which India is a leading player (a major exporter of software and IT/business services, with cities like Bengaluru as global IT hubs). Other Indian strengths include its large pool of skilled, English-speaking manpower, its entrepreneurial private sector, its capital markets and banking, and its democracy. (India's service-led, IT-driven growth contrasts with China's manufacturing-led growth.) So, while China leads in manufacturing, India has a distinctive strength in IT/services. Understanding India's IT/software strength is a prelims-relevant point. India's areas of strength include its globally competitive information technology (IT) and software services sector.

stem: In Pakistan, a large share of the economy and employment depends on __________ (as in India, but even more so).
solution: In Pakistan, a large share of the economy and employment depends on agriculture — agriculture (and the agriculture-based industries, like textiles) is a mainstay of Pakistan's economy, contributing a significant share of its GDP and employing a large part of its workforce. This heavy dependence on agriculture (which is subject to the ups and downs of weather and prices) is one of the features (and vulnerabilities) of Pakistan's economy. (India too has a large agricultural workforce, but its economy is more diversified — with a bigger industrial and, especially, service sector.) Understanding Pakistan's heavy dependence on agriculture is a prelims-relevant point. In Pakistan, a large share of the economy and employment depends on agriculture.

stem: Comparing countries' development is useful because it allows each country to __________.
options: learn from the successes and failures of others (and understand what strategies work)
solution: Comparing the development experiences of different countries (like India, China, and Pakistan) is useful because it allows each country to learn from the successes and failures of the others — to see which development strategies and policies have worked well (and why), and which have not, and to understand the reasons behind different outcomes. By studying how other, comparable countries developed (their choices, strengths, and mistakes), a country can draw useful lessons for its own development policy (adopting what works and avoiding what does not, while adapting to its own conditions). So comparison is a way of learning and improving development strategy. Understanding why comparing development experiences is useful is a prelims-relevant point. Comparing countries' development is useful because it lets each country learn from the successes and failures of others.

stem: India has now become the __________ populous country in the world (recently overtaking China).
solution: India has now become the most populous country in the world (recently, around 2023, overtaking China to become No. 1 in population). This happened because India's population continued to grow (its birth rate, though falling, remained higher), while China's population growth slowed sharply (and its population began to plateau/decline) as a result of China's strict one-child policy and low fertility. So India is now the world's most populous country, and China the second. This huge (and now largest) population is central to India's development challenges and its potential (a vast workforce and market). Understanding that India is now the most populous country is a prelims-relevant point. India has now become the most populous country in the world, recently overtaking China.

stem: On the whole, the ranking of the three countries on economic growth and human development has generally been:
solution: On the whole, the ranking of the three countries on economic growth and on human development has generally been: China at the top (the fastest-growing, and the best on human-development indicators like life expectancy and literacy), followed by India (which has grown well, especially after 1991, and has moderate human-development indicators), and then Pakistan (which has grown more slowly and erratically, and lags on some human-development measures). So the broad ranking is China > India > Pakistan on these development measures (though the picture varies by specific indicator, and India and Pakistan are closer to each other than to China). Understanding this general ranking is a prelims point. On economic growth and human development, the general ranking is China (highest), then India, then Pakistan.

stem: One reason India's growth has created fewer jobs than China's is that India's growth has been led by __________, which is less job-creating than China's manufacturing.
solution: One reason India's growth has created fewer jobs than China's is that India's growth has been led largely by the service sector (and by capital-intensive industries) — especially skill-intensive services like IT, which employ mainly the highly-skilled and create relatively few jobs overall — whereas China's growth was led by manufacturing, which is much more labour-absorbing (it created huge numbers of jobs for less-skilled workers moving out of agriculture). So China's manufacturing-led growth generated far more employment (absorbing its surplus rural labour into factories) than India's more service- and capital-intensive growth. This is one reason India has faced the problem of 'jobless growth' relative to China. Understanding this (India's service-led growth = fewer jobs than China's manufacturing) is a prelims point. India's growth created fewer jobs than China's because it was led by services (and capital-intensive sectors), which are less job-creating than China's manufacturing.

stem: The comparison highlights that a country can achieve high growth but still have __________ if the growth does not reach all the people.
solution: The comparison of development experiences highlights that a country can achieve high economic growth but still have persistent poverty and inequality — if the benefits of that growth do not reach all the people (especially the poor) and are unevenly distributed. High GDP growth does not automatically translate into the elimination of poverty or into equality; the fruits of growth can be captured mainly by the better-off, or concentrated in certain regions/sectors, leaving many people poor and the gap between rich and poor widening. This is seen in both China and India (which have grown fast but still have poverty and rising inequality). So growth must be inclusive (reaching and benefiting all sections) for it to translate into genuine development. Understanding this (growth ≠ automatic end to poverty/inequality) is a prelims point. High growth can coexist with persistent poverty and inequality if the growth does not reach all the people.

stem: The development experiences suggest that investing in the __________ of the people (health, education) is crucial for long-term development.
solution: The development experiences (especially China's success) suggest that investing in the human capital / capabilities of the people — their health, education, and skills — is crucial for long-term, sustained development. China's heavy early investment in the health and education of its people gave it the healthy, educated, skilled workforce that could drive its rapid growth after the reforms. This underlines a key lesson: that developing the people (human capital) is not just a social good but an economic necessity for growth and development — a country's people are its most important resource. (This connects to the human-development perspective — development is about, and depends on, expanding people's capabilities and well-being.) Understanding that investing in human capital is crucial for development is a prelims point. The development experiences suggest that investing in the human capital (health, education) of the people is crucial for long-term development.

stem: Pakistan's economic growth has been described as __________ (going up and down), partly due to political instability and reliance on foreign aid.
solution: Pakistan's economic growth has been described as fluctuating (erratic) and unstable — going up and down over the years, rather than being steady and sustained. This instability has been due to factors such as: political instability (frequent changes of government, and periods of military rule, leading to inconsistent policies); the volatility of its agriculture-dependent economy; a heavy reliance on foreign aid, loans, and remittances (unstable external sources); low investment in human development; and periodic economic and security crises. So, unlike China's steady high growth or India's fairly steady growth, Pakistan's growth has been up-and-down and less reliable. Understanding that Pakistan's growth has been fluctuating/erratic is a prelims-relevant point. Pakistan's growth has been fluctuating/erratic and unstable, partly due to political instability and reliance on foreign aid.

stem: A key point from the human-development perspective (associated with economists like Amartya Sen) is that development should ultimately expand people's __________.
options: freedoms and capabilities (their real opportunities to live the lives they value)
solution: A key point from the human-development perspective (strongly associated with the economist and Nobel laureate Amartya Sen) is that development should ultimately be about expanding people's freedoms and capabilities — that is, expanding the real opportunities and abilities that people have to live the kind of lives they value and have reason to value (to be healthy, educated, nourished, and able to participate in society and make choices). In this view, development is not just about raising incomes/GDP, but about enhancing human well-being and the real freedoms of people. This perspective (development as freedom/capability expansion) underlies the emphasis on human development (health, education, etc.) in judging and comparing the progress of countries. Understanding this human-development/capability view (Amartya Sen) is a prelims-relevant point. Development should ultimately expand people's freedoms and capabilities — their real opportunities to live the lives they value (Amartya Sen's view).

stem: Which of the following is a common feature/challenge shared by India, China, and Pakistan?
options: having large populations and having started development around the same time (facing challenges of poverty and development)
solution: A common feature shared by India, China, and Pakistan is that all three are large (populous) developing countries that started their development journeys at around the same time (the late 1940s), and all faced (and to varying degrees still face) the common challenges of a developing country — such as widespread poverty, the need to develop their economies, large agrarian populations, and the tasks of industrialising, providing employment, and improving the health, education, and living standards of huge populations. This common starting point and set of challenges is exactly what makes comparing their different development paths and outcomes meaningful. Understanding these shared features/challenges is a prelims point. India, China, and Pakistan share large populations, a common late-1940s start to development, and the challenges of poverty and development.

stem: One reason for choosing to COMPARE India with China and Pakistan (rather than with, say, the USA) is that these three countries:
options: had broadly similar starting points and are all developing countries, making the comparison meaningful
solution: One reason for choosing to compare India with China and Pakistan (rather than with a very different, already-developed country like the USA) is that these three countries had broadly similar starting points (all were poor, largely agrarian, developing countries that began their development around the same time — the late 1940s) and are all developing countries facing similar kinds of challenges. This similarity makes the comparison meaningful and instructive — because they started from a comparable base, the differences in their later outcomes can be attributed largely to the differences in their development strategies and choices (which is what we want to learn from). Comparing with a country like the USA (with a totally different history, level of development, and conditions) would be far less instructive for this purpose. Understanding why these three are compared (similar starting points) is a prelims point. India, China, and Pakistan are compared because they had broadly similar starting points and are all developing countries, making the comparison meaningful.

stem: China's growth model relied heavily on high rates of __________ (saving and building factories, infrastructure) to fuel its rapid expansion.
solution: China's growth model relied heavily on very high rates of investment (and saving) — China saved a very large share of its income and invested it heavily in building factories, infrastructure (roads, railways, ports, power), housing, and productive capacity. This high investment rate (among the highest in the world) rapidly expanded the country's productive capacity and infrastructure, fuelling its very rapid economic growth. (High saving and investment are, as the Harrod-Domar model notes, key to growth — and China's exceptionally high investment rate was central to its exceptional growth.) India too has raised its investment rate, but not to China's very high levels. Understanding that China's growth relied on high investment is a prelims-relevant point. China's growth relied heavily on very high rates of investment (saving and building factories/infrastructure) to fuel its rapid expansion.

stem: In terms of the sectoral shift of the workforce, China moved a large part of its workforce out of agriculture into __________ faster than India did.
solution: In terms of the sectoral shift of the workforce, China moved a large part of its workforce out of agriculture into manufacturing/industry (and to some extent services) faster and more successfully than India did. China's manufacturing boom (and its Township and Village Enterprises and SEZs) absorbed huge numbers of workers moving out of agriculture into factory (industrial) jobs — a rapid structural transformation of employment. India's shift of workers out of agriculture has been slower and less complete (and more toward services than manufacturing), so a larger share of India's workforce has remained in agriculture. This faster shift into manufacturing was part of China's success in growth and job creation. Understanding this difference (China's faster shift into manufacturing) is a prelims point. China moved a large part of its workforce out of agriculture into manufacturing/industry faster than India did.

stem: The comparison of India, China, and Pakistan shows that there is no single, fixed path to development; rather, outcomes depend on each country's:
options: policies, strategies, and investments (the choices it makes)
solution: The comparison of India, China, and Pakistan shows that there is no single, fixed, or automatic path to development — the three countries, starting from broadly similar points, took different routes and achieved different outcomes. This illustrates that development outcomes depend heavily on each country's policies, strategies, and investments — the choices it makes: how it structures its economy (e.g., manufacturing-led vs service-led), when and how it reforms, how much it invests in human capital (health, education) and infrastructure, how it handles population, its political system, and so on. So a country's development is shaped by its own decisions and efforts (not predetermined), which is why studying these choices (and their results) across countries is so valuable. Understanding this (development depends on policy choices) is a prelims point. The comparison shows there is no single path to development — outcomes depend on each country's policies, strategies, and investments (its choices).

stem: India can learn from China's experience the importance of building __________ and manufacturing to create jobs, while China (and others) can learn from India's __________.
options: infrastructure/human capital and a strong manufacturing base; democratic institutions and IT/services strength
solution: The comparison offers mutual lessons. India can learn from China's experience the importance of building strong infrastructure and human capital, and a robust manufacturing base — which China used to grow fast and create huge numbers of jobs (addressing India's weaknesses in these areas and its problem of jobless growth). At the same time, China (and others) can learn from India's strengths — such as its democratic institutions (political freedom, participation, and accountability, achieved alongside development), and its success in IT and services and its entrepreneurial private sector. So each country has both strengths to share and weaknesses to work on — which is the value of comparing their experiences (learning from one another). Understanding these mutual lessons is a prelims-relevant point. India can learn from China's infrastructure, human capital, and manufacturing; China/others can learn from India's democratic institutions and IT/services strengths.

stem: Ultimately, the comparison underscores that the real measure of a country's development is the __________ of its people.
options: well-being and quality of life (human development)
solution: Ultimately, the comparison of India, China, and Pakistan underscores that the real, true measure of a country's development is the well-being and quality of life of its people (their human development) — how healthy, educated, secure, and prosperous the people are, and how free they are to live good lives — not merely the size of the GDP or the growth rate. A country's development should be judged by whether it improves the lives of its people (all of them, including the poor) — reducing poverty, improving health and education, and expanding people's opportunities and freedoms. So human welfare/development is the ultimate goal and yardstick of development (a central lesson of the chapter). Understanding this (human well-being as the real measure of development) is a key prelims point. The real measure of a country's development is the well-being and quality of life (human development) of its people, not just its GDP.

stem: Assertion (A): China's growth has been more employment-generating than India's. Reason (R): China's growth was driven by labour-intensive manufacturing, whereas India's was driven more by capital- and skill-intensive services. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that China's growth has been more employment-generating (job-creating) than India's. And the reason is (R) that China's growth was driven largely by labour-intensive manufacturing (factories that employ large numbers of workers, absorbing the surplus labour from agriculture), whereas India's growth was driven more by capital-intensive and skill-intensive services (like IT), which employ relatively fewer, more-skilled workers and create fewer jobs overall. Because manufacturing absorbs far more labour than capital-/skill-intensive services, China's manufacturing-led growth created more jobs than India's service-led growth — so R correctly explains A. Understanding this reasoning is a prelims point. China's growth generated more employment than India's because it was driven by labour-intensive manufacturing, whereas India's was driven by capital-/skill-intensive services.

stem: In the composition of exports, China exports mainly __________, reflecting its manufacturing strength.
solution: In the composition of its exports, China exports mainly manufactured goods (industrial products) — such as electronics, machinery, textiles, toys, and a vast range of other manufactured items — reflecting its enormous manufacturing strength (its position as the 'factory of the world'). This export of manufactures (higher-value industrial goods) in huge quantities is central to China's trade surpluses and economic strength. (India, by comparison, exports a mix that includes services — like IT/software — and various goods; and a developing country that exports mainly raw materials/primary products, rather than manufactures, is generally at a disadvantage.) So China's export basket being dominated by manufactures reflects its industrial/manufacturing-led development. Understanding that China exports mainly manufactured goods is a prelims-relevant point. China exports mainly manufactured goods (industrial products), reflecting its manufacturing strength.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours' is that:
options: Comparing India with China and Pakistan (which started developing at around the same time) shows that different development strategies lead to different outcomes — China achieved the fastest growth and best human-development record (aided by early investment in human capital and infrastructure), India grew well (especially after 1991) but lags on human development, and Pakistan grew more slowly — teaching that development requires not just growth but investment in people and that it must be judged by human welfare
Growth is the only thing that matters
solution: The chapter conveys that comparing the development experiences of India with its two major neighbours — China and Pakistan — which all started their development journeys at around the same time (the late 1940s), is instructive, because it shows how different development strategies and choices lead to different outcomes. China (which reformed and opened up its economy in 1978, well before India's 1991 reforms and Pakistan's 1988 reforms, and which had earlier invested heavily in infrastructure and human capital — education and health, and controlled its population through the one-child policy, all under a one-party communist system) achieved the fastest and most sustained economic growth (becoming a manufacturing and economic superpower) and the best record on human-development indicators (life expectancy, literacy, etc.). India also grew well (especially after its 1991 reforms, with a service-led growth), and is a democracy, but it lags behind China on many human-development measures and on job creation, and it has a faster-growing population. Pakistan grew more slowly and erratically, hampered by political instability, over-dependence on agriculture and a narrow export base, and reliance on foreign aid/remittances and low human-development investment. The comparison teaches important lessons: that rapid, sustained growth requires not just economic reforms but also strong investment in people (human capital — education and health) and infrastructure (as China did); and, crucially, that development must be judged not by economic growth (GDP) alone but by improvements in human welfare and human development (health, education, poverty reduction, and quality of life) — and that all these countries, despite their growth, still face challenges of poverty, inequality, and environmental degradation. Understanding these comparative development experiences and the lessons they hold is the central concern of this chapter. Comparing India, China, and Pakistan shows that different strategies bring different outcomes — China grew fastest with the best human development (aided by early investment in people and infrastructure), India grew well but lags on human development, and Pakistan grew slowly — teaching that development needs investment in people and must be judged by human welfare, not growth alone.
